The best three words in sports are "Win or go home". Everything is on the line here after the Phillies rallied to win Game 2. Their season was on life support until Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hit back-to-back homers to tie the game in the 7th, and Alec Bohm hit the go-ahead homer in the 10th.
The burning question for manager Don Mattingly: Who pitches? Zack Wheeler or Aaron Nola? The answer feels obvious: go with Wheeler, the staff's ace. It would be four days between starts and three days of rest for Wheeler.
Wheeler boasts a 3.00 ERA, a 2.86 xERA, and a 3.35 FIP. He's a strikeout machine, punching out 10.72 per nine, but his walk rate has grown to 2.61 this year. He's rounding into prime form at the best time, pitching to a 1.71 ERA in five September outings.
Diving into the Phillies' pen usage, everything is on the table. The Phillies can add two extra weapons to their pen, with Aaron Nola and Jesus Luzardo as options. Andrew Painter threw 37 pitches in game two — so he might not be an option for Mattingly. The good news? Jhoan Duran will be an option since Painter saved the pen on Wednesday.
Offensively, the Phillies looked rough in the stretch entering the playoffs, but all it takes is one or two long balls to shift this game in their direction.
So far in the Wild Card round, Alec Bohm has been the guy for the Phillies, leading them with a .375 average and a 1.319 OPS. Schwarber and Harper are always a threat, but Bohm playing this well gives Philly a boost.

- CF Michael Harris II
- SS Mauricio Dubón
- LF Mike Yastrzemski
- 3B Austin Riley
- 2B Ozzie Albies
- DH Dominic Smith
While the Phillies have multiple strong starter options for a do-or-die Game 3, the Braves have zero rotation depth, and it's showing. The options are a full bullpen game or an opener before Grant Holmes, or Grant Holmes on a short leash.
None of those are ideal options in this spot. The basic stats indicate Holmes had a solid year, posting a 3.44 ERA, but his 5.04 xERA and 4.67 FIP are terrifying in a playoff game. Holmes isn't a swing-and-miss pitcher, striking out just 6.8 hitters per nine innings, and when you can't strike hitters out, they get more chances to do damage.
Holmes also gets hit very hard, ranking in the 1st percentile in average exit velocity and third in hard-hit rate.
In this series, the Braves bats have been more reliable than the Phillies in the middle-to-bottom of the order. However, the top of the order has destroyed them. It starts with Ronald Acuna Jr. with no hits, Drake Baldwin hitting .222, and Matt Olson hitting .125.
Putting it lightly, the Braves will face an uphill battle winning this game if their three best hitters don't hit.
Sure, the Phillies totally limped into the playoffs, but the Braves have some glaring issues of their own, and they're showing up at the worst time. The lineup has been unreliable, and the rotation is a mess.
I want Wheeler or even Nola if he's starting. The Braves have no pitching answers to contain the Philadelphia big boppers.

item.content:encoded:
Thin MLB crowds in Atlanta, Houston show challenge of selling afternoon Wild Card Series tickets
A late home run secured a playoff win for Atlanta; stadium attendance remains low for scheduled weekday afternoon games
- 1 minuto de lectura'
Austin Riley delivered the first clutch moment of Major League Baseball's playoffs on Tuesday, hitting a go-ahead three-run homer in the eighth inning that pushed the Atlanta Braves over the Philadelphia Phillies for a 5-3 win .
It was an electric scene for fans at Truist Park — at least for those who decided to show up.
There has been a noticeable number of empty seats in Atlanta and Houston for day games during this week's Wild Card Series, with the Braves drawing 30,127 fans for Game 1 on Tuesday that started at 2 p.m. local time, well below the 41,108 capacity. The Astros announced that 34,011 fans attended Tuesday's 4 p.m. Game 1 at Daikin Park, also well below its 41,168-seat limit.
It's not the first time this has happened.
Since MLB permanently expanded the playoffs to a 12-team bracket in 2022, just six of 26 afternoon Wild Card Series games through Tuesday have reached or exceeded stadium capacity. Seven games failed to reach even 85% capacity. The Braves-Phillies game on Tuesday was 73.2% full, which is the lowest since the postseason expanded, according to research from Sportradar.
Game 2 of the Braves-Phillies series had an announced crowd of 37,150 on Wednesday.
The main issue for day games is obvious: It's hard for fans to attend day games during the week — particularly in late September and October — because people have to work and children are back in school. It doesn't help that those game times are announced with only a few days' notice.
Still, it's a less-than-ideal atmosphere for some of the most important contests of the year.
Phillies third baseman Alec Bohm shrugged off the smaller crowds before Wednesday's game, saying his team just wants to win games and advance.
“I don’t think anybody on our team is really focused on how many people are showing up here," Bohm said. "It’s just kind of -- I think, like you said, it’s a 2 o’clock game in the middle of the week, so I think that might have something to do with it.
“That doesn’t take away from what’s going on on the field and kind of the stakes of all that in our minds.”
All three ALWCS games in Cleveland last year between the Guardians and Detroit Tigers started at 1:08 p.m., and none drew more than 30,000 fans. The Tampa Bay Rays had just 19,704 for an ALWCS opener against Texas in 2023 that started at 3:08 p.m., the lowest attendance for a non-COVID MLB postseason game since the 1919 World Series.
MLB declined to comment on the attendance numbers, but the league spreads its wild-card games throughout the day on purpose so they have their own television window and capture the largest viewing audience possible. NBC is paying the league roughly $200 million per year to host “Sunday Night Baseball” and the Wild Card Series during a three-year deal agreed to last November.
The Astros fans who did attend Tuesday's game were in a bit of a foul mood, peppering the team with boos as they fell behind 5-0 by the fifth inning on the way to a 6-3 loss. Astros manager Joe Espada said he understood the fans' frustration but hoped for a better atmosphere on Wednesday.
“I do want our fans to know that we love them and we need them,” Espada said. “They’re part of what we are trying to accomplish here. They’re part of our family.”
AP Sports Writers Charles Odum in Atlanta and Kristie Rieken in Houston contributed to this story.

The Los Angeles Dodgers have yet to begin their quest for a three-peat during these MLB playoffs, which are already underway, but on paper, LA is going to be a tough out regardless of its opponent.
However, even though the MLB playoffs are underway, it’s not too early to start thinking about the major offseason decision the team faces regarding ace starter Tarik Skubal.
Recently, in an MLB free agent predictions piece, Tarik Skubal is being linked back to the Los Angeles Dodgers on a 10-year deal.
More MLB on Heavy: Los Angeles Dodgers Announce 3 Sudden Roster Moves Amid MLB Playoffs
Dodgers Predicted to Retain Tarik Skubal
Back in August, the Dodgers shocked the MLB world by landing Tarik Skubal in a huge trade with the Detroit Tigers.
However, they (LA) face a big decision regarding his free-agent status, as he is set to hit the open market after the 2026 season.
BleacherReport.com’s Zach Buckley recently predicted LA to retain its new ace via a 10-year deal:
“Prediction: Skubal re-signs with the Dodgers on a 10-year deal.”
“In short, the crystal ball sees this coming down to the Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Mets—two of the biggest spenders in baseball. The Dodgers just made an aggressive move for Skubal at this year’s trade deadline, while the Mets badly need a boost to their rotation. This bidding war should be ferocious, but in the end, the Dodgers’ head start by having Skubal already on the roster could be what pushes them over the edge.”
More MLB on Heavy: MLB World Reacts to Austin Riley Moment in Phillies-Braves Game
Tarik Skubal Has Proved His Worth with Los Angeles
Let’s be clear: the 2X AL Cy Young winner in Tarik Skubal, doesn’t have to prove his worth to anybody, but since joining the Dodgers, he’s made it really hard for the team to ignore that he would be an immense addition to the starting rotation.
Across 10 starts with LA, Skubal holds a 2.61 ERA with 70 strikeouts.
He will be a huge piece to the Dodgers postseason fold, and if he really helps propel LA to a three-peat, that might be enough to truly force Andrew Friedman’s hand in his ongoing contract talks.
Dodgers fans, do you want to bring back Tarik Skubal? And at what price would you be willing to do so?

item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies traded for Luis Arraez to make their lineup deeper when they reached the MLB playoffs.
But now in the postseason, and facing elimination on Wednesday against the Atlanta Braves, the Phillies don’t even have Arraez available to play for them.
It’s an unfortunate reality, and it’s one the Phillies are going to have to navigate if they want to see Arraez put on their uniform again.
The Phillies lost the NL Wild Card Series opener on Tuesday to the Braves when Austin Riley hit a go-ahead home run for Atlanta in the eighth inning.
In a best-of-three series, it’s Wednesday or bust for the Phillies.
Arraez will only be able to watch and hope he gets another chance before Philadelphia’s season is over.
And given that Arraez’s contract expires after this season, he may never play for the Phillies again if they lose on Wednesday.
When is Luis Arraez Coming Back?
There’s no real clarity on Arraez’s return timeline yet.
The veteran sprained his left ankle on Thursday, Sept. 24, while running on the bases. He went down in a lot of pain and had to essentially be carried off the field.
The Phillies left him off of the NL Wild Card Series roster. Otto Kemp, a utility player with a great old-school baseball name, is on the roster for this series in Arraez’s place.
“We still get improvement every day, but not enough,” Mattingly told reporters on Monday about Arraez. “He was going to try to hit today and just wasn’t able to do it. So, we kind of crossed that bridge today.”
Arraez hadn’t swung a bat yet as of the time Mattingly spoke to reporters on Monday.
The contact wizard was also seen with a boot on his foot during the Phillies’ celebrations on Sunday after they clinched a playoff spot.
Arraez won’t be eligible to play against the Braves in the Wild Card Series since he was left off the roster.
That means that he can only play if the Phillies win the best-of-three series in Atlanta.
At that point, the Phillies would get the chance to name a Divisional Series roster. Players can be swapped in and out then, which would allow Arraez back into the mix if he’s ready.
Luis Arraez Stats
Arraez has been solid since coming to Philadelphia. He’s batted .278 with 10 doubles, two home runs and 21 RBI in 46 games.
He had been hitting .324 with the Giants before the trade.
He’s also made major strides as a second base defensive player in 2026, going from a negative there to a clear positive — although a sprained ankle might not help.
Arraez had settled into the cleanup spot for the Phillies — a very new-age decision to put the best contact hitter on the team at the 4-spot in the batting order. It was mostly working, though, and Philadelphia has to win without Arraez to give him another chance to get back in the lineup.

It’s do or die for the Phillies on Wednesday.
The Braves pushed them to the brink in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card with a 5-3 decision prompted by Austin Riley’s three-run shot in the eighth inning.
Another win in this series would mark first time the Braves prevailed over their NL East rivals in the postseason: the Phillies took the NLDS in both 2022 and 2023 and the 1993 NLCS over Atlanta.
This Phillies’ core has been chasing after a World Series throughout the decade, and another early exit will have its ramifications.
The onus to avoid that comes down to no one more than Bryce Harper, who struck out twice and went hitless Tuesday.
Phillies vs. Braves Game 2 prediction, best bet
Harper, who is a .269 postseason hitter in 58 games, narrowly missed a go-ahead two-run home run against Chris Sale in the sixth inning when the ball just sailed just right of the right-field pole.
He gets the lefty vs. righty matchup advantage against Atlanta’s Tyler Mahle, against whom he has posted a healthy .278/.350/.500 slash line.
Mahle leans on his four-seamer for nearly half of his pitches. He doesn’t throw it with extreme movement or overpowering velocity, averaging 92 mph, but he locates the strike zone with it well.
In the 14 four-seamers that Mahle served to Harper this season, Harper knocked two hits with a home run on eight swings, according to Statcast. Only two were whiffs.
In fact, Mahle wasn’t much of a swing-and-miss pitcher at all, ranking in only the 31 percentile.
That’s all while Harper remained an elite contact hitter, posting a .379 xwOBA, a Statcast metric that measures expected offensive production based on the exit velocity and launch angle of his contact rather than the results.
Harper has stated he loves playing at Truist Park, and his numbers say why.

item.content:encoded:
Game 1 of the AL Wild Card Series couldn't have gone much better for the Yankees. On the mound, Cam Schlittler was excellent, blanking the Red Sox for 6.1 impressive innings. Then, led by Ben Rice, the Yankees' offense plated nine runs, pulling away from Boston to go up 1-0 in the series.
Yesterday wasn't just the opening of the Yankees-Red Sox series, though. All three of the Wild Card matchups also got underway on Tuesday, so let's check in on what happened.
AL Wild Card Series Game 1
Chicago White Sox 6, Houston Astros 3
(Chicago leads 1-0)
After jumping out to a 3-0 lead early, the White Sox withstood the Astros and tacked on some more runs late to take the opener of the other AL matchup in Houston.
Facing an Astros' bullpen game, the White Sox got going quickly. With a runner on third in the first, Munetaka Murakami hit a fly ball that was deep enough for Chicago's Sam Antonacci to tag up and score. The next inning, Antonacci did it at the plate, hitting a bases loaded single to bring home two more runs. A Colson Montgomery homer in the fourth and a Chase Meidroth RBI single in the fifth had Chicago up big before Houston showed any resistance.
A two-run shot from Nelson Velázquez in the bottom of the fifth got the Astros on the board, but Chicago got one of those runs back a little while later. Houston countered with one in the eighth and brought the tying run to the plate, but couldn't cash in as the ChiSox held on from there. Amusingly, the Astros have now lost eight consecutive playoff games in Houston since early on in the 2023 playoffs. If Chicago can win one more at Daikin Park either today or tomorrow, they'll not only eliminate Houston but also secure their first playoff series victory since winning the 2005 World Series, over two decades ago. The Astros will have their best pitcher going for them in Hunter Brown, so we'll see if that's enough to keep their season alive.
NL Wild Card Series Game 1
Atlanta Braves 5, Philadelphia Phillies 3
(Atlanta leads 1-0)
Austin Riley's go-ahead eighth inning home run stunned the Phillies to give the Braves the series opener.
The Phillies opened the scoring early when Alec Bohm doubled home a run in the top of the first. Atlanta then answered back with Mike Yastrzemski RBI single. The game remained tied for a while after that as both Chris Sale and Jesús Luzardo put in solid outings; Luzardo hadn't necessarily been expected to even last five innings, as he was still relatively fresh off the IL and threw an inning of relief just to help the Phillies clinch a playof spot on Sunday. Things changed as both teams got to the bullpen, and there were some dramatic swings.
Atlanta took the lead for the first time in the sixth when Ozzie Albies hit an RBI triple thanks to some less-than-stellar fielding from Phillies' center fielder Derek Hill. However, a Ronald Acuña Jr. misplay in the seventh allowed J.T. Realmuto to hit a triple of his own, scoring two runs to put Philly back in front.
Phillies' manager Don Mattingly went for the kill shot by bringing on closer Jhoan Duran in the seventh. He got through that inning fine and came back out for the eighth, facing the heart of Atlanta's order. He got two quick outs before Michael Harris II kept the inning alive with a softly-struck infield single. Duran hit Albies with a pitch after that, bringing Riley to the plate. Duran then left a fastball right in the middle of the zone, and Riley took full advantage, giving Atlanta a lead that Raisel Iglesias held on to in the ninth.
If the Braves win today, then they'll advance to play the two-time defending champion Dodgers in the NLDS. If the Phillies can hold them off behind ace Cristopher Sánchez however, then Game 3 awaits on Thursday.
San Diego Padres 8, Chicago Cubs 0
(San Diego leads 1-0)
Michael King took a no-hitter into the seventh inning as the Padres' offense crushed Cubs pitching in the late night game out west.
The Cubs' story this season is that they have an excellent offense and poor pitching, ranking first and last in fWAR respectively. However in Game 1, only one of those things proved true. Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado both hit first inning home runs against Matthew Boyd, getting San Diego off to the perfect start, from which they only added on to their lead.
Meanwhile, the Cubs offense couldn't do much against King. The former Yankee didn't allow a hit until Nico Hoerner singled with one out in the seventh. In total, King shut out Chicago over seven frames, allowing just the one hit and three walks, striking out eight.
In the ninth inning, Padres' pitcher Joe Musgrove returned to the majors after a two-year absence while recovering from Tommy John surgery. He allowed a couple Cubs to reach base, but did end up throwing a scoreless inning.

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Austin Riley supported Chris Sale’s strong start, halted the Phillies’ postseason dominance of Atlanta and put six months of frustration behind him with a swing that could make October worth savoring for both him and the Braves.
Riley’s three-run homer off All-Star closer Jhoan Duran with two outs in the eighth inning gave the Braves a thrilling 5-3 win over the Phillies in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series on Tuesday afternoon at Truist Park.
“I’m happy for Austin Riley,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It’s been a tough year for him. But this just goes to show you, when the playoffs start, everything starts at zero. Nothing that happened in the regular season really matters. It’s a clean slate. Austin Riley has been a great postseason player.”
Four of Riley’s six career postseason homers have been of the go-ahead variety and three of those have been hit in the eighth inning or later. That eighth inning or later total matches Troy Glaus, Bernie Williams, Jose Altuve and Freddie Freeman for the most in MLB history.
The slugging third baseman previously hit a go-ahead shot in the ninth inning of Game 1 of the NLCS on Oct. 12, 2020, and he hit a go-ahead two-run home run with two outs in the bottom of the eighth in Game 2 of the 2023 NLDS, also against the Phillies. Chipper Jones is the only other Braves player with multiple go-ahead homers in the eighth inning or later of a postseason game.
“I know how my season went,” Riley said. “It’s not the way I wanted it to. But that's the beauty of the postseason. You get a clean slate and go out there and try to do something for the boys and for this city.”
Instead of talking about being on the brink of elimination, the Braves joyfully discussed how everything changed when Riley sent Duran’s 99.9 mph fastball over the right-center-field fence for a go-ahead home run.
Riley doesn’t remember what any of his teammates said after he returned to a jubilant dugout after his home run. Was he also in a haze as he rounded the bases?
“I remember my gum falling out of my mouth,” Riley said.
It was a jaw-dropping moment that put the Braves in an encouraging position.
In the history of the best-of-three Wild Card Series, teams taking a 1-0 lead have gone on to win the series 21 of 24 times (88%), including 17 two-game sweeps. Home teams have won all nine series in which they have gone ahead 1-0, including eight sweeps.
The Phillies had won six of the previous eight postseason games played against the Braves this decade. Philadelphia beat Atlanta in the 2022 and ‘23 NL Division Series.
“It doesn't get more fun than this, playing this game in the postseason,” Weiss said. “You can imagine going from losing the lead to something like that. The swinging emotions are enormous. What a big home run.”
Sale played a significant role in this crucial Game 1 victory. The Braves ace registered nine strikeouts over 6 1/3 innings. Two of the three runs he surrendered came via a J.T. Realmuto triple that Didier Fuentes surrendered with two outs in the seventh.
So where was Sale when the value of his strong effort was preserved by Riley’s home run?
“I was getting some arm care in, and unfortunately the [clubhouse] TV I was watching was on the delay [feed],” he said. “I just heard craziness coming from the entire clubhouse. Everyone's losing their mind, and I'm just sitting there like, ‘Oh, what's going on?’ About four seconds later, you see what happened. I just couldn't be happier for him.”
Coming off two injury-shortened seasons, Riley hit .219 with 19 homers and a .654 OPS during the regular season. Safe to say this was the most frustrating season of the two-time All-Star’s career. This past weekend in Miami, he talked about how relaxing his right shoulder might have helped him hit two homers in last week’s Reds series.
The triple came against a 98.2 mph splitter that was in the middle of the zone. The ball had 109 mph exit velocity and it traveled a Statcast-projected 394 feet.
This home run came against a 99.9 mph four-seamer that was middle in. This is the hardest-thrown pitch Riley has homered against in his career, besting a homer he hit against Jacob deGrom’s 99.7 mph heater on July 1, 2021.
This latest home run had a 104.6 mph exit velocity and it traveled a projected 385 feet.
It would have been a home run in 27 of 30 MLB ballparks. Did Riley know it was gone?
“No, I did not,” he said. “I was just praying as I was running to first.”

ATLANTA -- While most of the Phillies filtered down the tunnel toward the visitors’ clubhouse following Tuesday afternoon’s stunning loss to the Braves, Cristopher Sánchez lingered briefly in the dugout.
"I saw him at the end of the game," said Phillies designated hitter Kyle Schwarber, "and it just looked like he was staring out there at the mound. So I think that he knows what he's going to be tasked with for tomorrow."
That task is simple: Keep Philadelphia’s season alive.
It won’t be easy for the Phillies following their 5-3 loss to the Braves in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series at Truist Park. They now need to win back-to-back games to avoid elimination -- something only three of the previous 24 teams to lose Game 1 in a best-of-three Wild Card Series have managed to do (2020 Padres, 2020 Athletics, 2025 Yankees).
If the Phillies have any hopes of becoming the fourth, it all starts on Wednesday afternoon with Sánchez on the hill.
"I just try to be my best self every time I'm out there on the mound and try to go out there and compete every time that I can," Sánchez said via interpreter Diego D'Aniello. "It's a short series, so it's just about going out there and putting as many zeros on the board as I can. On my end, it's about being able to put the team in a good position to win."
Sánchez certainly does that more often than not.
He continued his emergence as one of the game's best pitchers this season by putting together another Cy Young-caliber campaign after finishing as the runner-up last season to Pirates ace Paul Skenes.
As for this year, Sánchez ranked second in the NL in strikeouts (231), second in innings pitched (207) and sixth in ERA (2.91). He did not allow a run for the entire month of May as part of his historic 50 2/3-inning scoreless streak.
But all that matters now is what he does in Game 2.
"Always feel good with Cristopher out there," Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said. "The playoffs are momentum-based, it seems like, and really, momentum starts with your starting pitcher."
Now, while the Phillies have the utmost confidence in Sánchez regardless of the mound he's pitching from, it's hard to ignore what he's done pitching on the road compared to pitching within the comforts of Citizens Bank Park.
Sánchez has talked often about how much he loves pitching at home -- and for good reason. He went 12-3 with a 2.23 ERA in 19 home starts this season. He was 6-0 with a 1.94 ERA at home last season.
But on the road?
Sánchez went 6-4 with a 3.87 ERA this season. His career road ERA (3.92) is more than a full run higher than it is at home (2.60).
"It's just about remaining calm and remaining focused when you're about to hit the field," Sánchez said of his Game 2 assignment. "It's about keeping focus on what we do on the field."
Sánchez, of course, also has plenty of familiarity with the Braves.
He's faced them nine times (eight starts) in his career. Four of those starts have come over the past two seasons.
But he has never beaten Atlanta. Sánchez is 0-5 against the Braves -- though that mark may be a bit deceiving. Despite the ugly record, he has a respectable 3.26 ERA in those nine outings, including a 2.19 ERA in four meetings since the start of last season.
That said, some of Atlanta's best hitters have given Sánchez some trouble in the past. Matt Olson, Ozzie Albies, Ronald Acuña Jr. and Austin Riley are a combined 28-for-72 (.389) against the Phillies' co-ace.
But again, none of that matters come Wednesday.
All that matters is what Sánchez does once he takes the mound. The same mound he was so locked in on before departing the ballpark on Tuesday evening.
"Just trying to get a little taste of what it will be like being out there tomorrow," Schwarber said. "Any time he takes the ball for us, we're always excited for that, and we're excited to get out here tomorrow and play a game.
"Let's go. You know what I mean? That's our guy."

First baseman Pete Alonso of the Baltimore Orioles has been named the American League Player of the Week, and third baseman Nolan Arenado of the Arizona Diamondbacks has been selected the National League Player of the Week. The announcements were made earlier today on MLB Network.
Alonso earned the honor for the seventh time in his career and second time this season after winning his first award in the AL with the Orioles on August 17th. He previously won five times during his tenure with the New York Mets, including June 24, 2019; September 26, 2022; July 30, 2023; April 15, 2024; and June 9, 2025. Alonso is the 12th player ever to garner honors in at least five consecutive seasons, regardless of team or league, joining Hall of Famer Vladimir Guerrero (8 seasons, 1998-2005); Manny Ramirez (7 seasons, 1997-2003); Arenado (6 seasons, 2014-2019); Aaron Judge (6 seasons, 2020-2025); George Bell (5 seasons, 1986-1990); Miguel Cabrera (5 seasons, 2012-2016); Hall of Famer Andre Dawson (5 seasons, 1987-1991); Carlos Delgado (5 seasons, 2000-2004); Clayton Kershaw (5 seasons, 2011-2015); Albert Pujols (5 seasons, 2005-2009); and Gary Sheffield (5 seasons, 1992-96). Arenado earned his ninth career award and first as a member of the Diamondbacks, marking Arizona’s fourth award of the year in addition to his teammates Ildemaro Vargas (April 27th); Ketel Marte (May 26th) and Corbin Carroll (August 17th). Arenado previously won six times as a member of the Colorado Rockies between 2014-2019 and twice as a member of the St. Louis Cardinals in 2022, including August 24, 2014; June 28, 2015; April 18, 2016; July 24, 2017; June 25, 2018; May 27, 2019; April 11, 2022; and August 8, 2022. He is the 31st player with at least nine awards in his career and just the eighth with at least nine awards in the National League, joining Barry Bonds (15); Pujols (13); Hall of Famer Mike Piazza (12); Sammy Sosa (11); Freddie Freeman (10); Hall of Famer Tony Gwynn (10); and Sheffield (9).
- The 31-year-old hit .389 (7-for-18) with five homers, eight RBI, three walks, eight runs scored, a 1.222 slugging percentage and a .500 on-base percentage across five contests.
- The Tampa, Florida native led the Majors in homers, slugging, OPS (1.722) and total bases (22); ranked second in runs scored; tied for third in RBI; and tied for fifth in on-base percentage.
- The five-time All-Star opened his week with a two-homer game against the Blue Jays on Monday and hit a pair of longballs in the first game of a doubleheader at Yankee Stadium on Friday. Alonso now has 29 career multi-homer games which are third-most in the Majors since his debut in 2019 behind only Aaron Judge (40 G) and Kyle Schwarber (36 G).
- The 2019 Jackie Robinson NL Rookie of the Year also slugged a home run in the first game of a doubleheader on Wednesday against Toronto as he finished his year with 43 homers and 113 RBI. Per Elias, he became the first player since RBI became official in 1920 to lead the AL and NL in RBI for a single season after he led the NL with 131 RBI in 2022. Additionally, he is the eighth Orioles player to lead the league in RBI and the first since Chris Davis had 138 RBI in 2013.
- The 2025 Silver Slugger crossed the 40-homer threshold with his two-homer game on Monday, marking his fourth season of at least 40 home runs, joining 2019 (53 HR); 2022 (40 HR); and 2023 (46 HR). His 43 homers are third-most by a Baltimore player in their first season with the club, behind Hall of Famer Frank Robinson (49 HR in 1966) and Mark Trumbo (47 HR in 2016). Alonso, who has played in 577 consecutive games since June 18, 2023, became the first Oriole to start every game of a season since Jonathan Schoop in 2016.
- The 35-year-old hit .435 (10-for-23) with three homers, eight RBI, two doubles, two walks, seven runs scored, a stolen base, a .913 slugging percentage and a .519 on-base percentage in six games.
- The Newport Beach, California native tied for second in total bases (21) and hits; ranked third in on-base percentage and OPS (1.432); tied for third in slugging, RBI and runs scored; and tied for fifth in batting average.
- The eight-time All-Star slugged a homer on Tuesday and Thursday at Colorado before also going deep on Friday at San Diego, marking his 30th homer of the year. It marked the eighth time in his career that he hit at least 30 homers, and his eight seasons of at least 30 home runs are third-most by a primary third baseman (min. 100 GS at 3B in season), behind only Hall of Famers Mike Schmidt (12 seasons of 30+ HR) and Eddie Mathews (10 seasons of 30+ HR).
- The 10-time Rawlings Gold Glover and six-time Platinum Glove Award winner finished his season on a 13-game hitting streak that dates back to September 13th, and he hit safely in 18 of his final 20 games of the season. During the stretch, he slashed .420/.463/.840 with six homers, 16 RBI and a 1.303 OPS. Arenado’s hitting streak is the fourth-longest by a Diamondbacks player to end a season, trailing only Paul Goldschmidt (19 G in 2013); Chad Tracy (14 G in 2005); and Tony Womack (14 G in 1999).
- The five-time Silver Slugger reached base safely in each of his last 21 games, matching Luis Gonzalez (2001) for the longest streak to end a season in franchise history. Overall, his 21-game on-base streak is the fifth-longest single season on-base streak of his career behind a 30-game streak in 2014, a 25-gamer in 2024 and a pair of 24-gamers in 2024 and 2018.
Other noteworthy NL performances last week included starting pitcher Jared Jones (1-0, 0.00 ERA, 2 GS, 11.0 IP, 2 H, 0 BB, 14 SO) of the Pittsburgh Pirates; starting pitcher Eury Pérez (1-0, 0.00 ERA, 1 GS, 10.0 IP, 1 H, 1 BB, 11 SO) of the Miami Marlins; infielder Bryson Stott (.474, 2 RBI, 6 2B, 5 BB, 4 R, .789 SLG, .583 OBP) of the Philadelphia Phillies; rookie outfielder Carson Benge (.440, 1 HR, 4 RBI, 3 2B, 3 BB, 5 R, .680 SLG, .500 OBP) of the New York Mets; second baseman Brice Turang (.360, 2 HR, 7 RBI, 3 2B, 1 BB, 5 R, .720 SLG) and outfielder Jackson Chourio (.471, 1 HR, 5 RBI, 3 BB, 7 R, 2 SB, .647 SLG, .550 OBP) of the Milwaukee Brewers; the 2026 Tony Gwynn NL Batting Champion, catcher Gabriel Moreno (.400, 1 HR, 8 RBI, 1 2B, 1 3B, 2 BB, 5 R, .600 SLG, .435 OBP) of the Arizona Diamondbacks; and utilityman Mauricio Dubón (.368, 1 HR, 3 RBI, 1 BB, 3 R, 1 SB, .526 SLG, .400 OBP) of the Atlanta Braves.
Other noteworthy AL performances last week included rookie outfielder Lucas Spence (.333, 4 HR, 9 RBI, 1 2B, 1 3B, 4 BB, 5 R, 1.167 SLG, .455 OBP), the 2026 AL Rod Carew Batting Champion, All-Star outfielder Yordan Alvarez (.375, 2 HR, 7 RBI, 2 2B, 4 BB, 7 R, .708 SLG, .483 OBP) and first baseman Christian Walker (.348, 4 HR, 7 RBI, 1 2B, 3 BB, 7 R, .913 SLG, .407 OBP); utilityman Luke Keaschall (.381, 1 HR, 6 RBI, 2 2B, 1 3B, 3 BB, 10 R, 1 SB, .905 SLG, .462 OBP) of the Minnesota Twins; closer Cade Smith (0.00 ERA, 3 G, 2 SV, 2.2 IP, 0 H, 1 BB, 4 SO) of the Cleveland Guardians; first baseman Vinnie Pasquantino (.333, 3 HR, 9 RBI, 2 2B, 1 BB, 6 R, .792 SLG, .385 OBP) and outfielder Jac Caglianone (.455, 4 RBI, 5 2B, 4 R, .682 SLG, .455 OBP) of the Kansas City Royals; outfielder Wade Meckler (.435, 2 RBI, 1 2B, 3 BB, 3 R, .565 SLG, .480 OBP) of the Los Angeles Angels; and All-Star first baseman Munetaka Murakami (.292, 3 HR, 7 RBI, 2 2B, 2 BB, 5 R, .750 SLG, .370 OBP) and second baseman Chase Meidroth (.615, 1 HR, 5 RBI, 2 2B, 1 BB, 3 R, 1.000 SLG, .643 OBP) of the Chicago White Sox.
Atlanta Braves right fielder Ronald Acuña Jr. earned his fourth career Play of the Week Award, after previously winning on August 19, 2019; August 8, 2022; and July 21, 2025. Overall, it is the 13th honor for the Braves since the inception of the award in 2019 with Acuña’s four awards joined by honors to Charlie Culberson (7/8/2019); Nick Markakis (7/15/2019); Adam Duvall (9/8/2020); Tyler Matzek (5/10/2021); a joint award to Ozzie Albies and Orlando Arcia (7/3/2023); Austin Riley (8/19/2024); Michael Harris II (9/3/2024); Jurickson Profar (8/11/2025); and Jim Jarvis (5/11/2026). With no outs and the Braves leading the Marlins 1-0 in the second inning, Heriberto Hernández hit a ball towards the wall as Acuña made a leaping catch to take away extra-bases. The best time of the baseball year is finally here. The playoffs begin Tuesday, with a quadruple-header of wild-card games on tap. The schedule for each series' first two games is identical.
Let's break down how each team got here, how they can win, X-factors, series predictions and more before the wild-card round begins.
AL: CWS-HOU • BOS-NYY | NL: PHI-ATL • CHC-SD
No. 6 Philadelphia Phillies vs. No. 3 Atlanta Braves
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 2 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Jesús Luzardo (PHI) vs. Chris Sale (ATL)
Game 2, 2 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Cristopher Sánchez (PHI) vs. Tyler Mahle (ATL)
Game 3, TBD*: Aaron Nola (or Zack Wheeler on four days' rest) (PHI) vs. Grant Holmes (ATL)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Phillies: It was a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde type of season for the Phillies, to say the least. For the second time in five seasons, an in-season managerial firing was needed to light a fire under an underperforming veteran roster that appeared to be letting their window close. But the Phillies, like they've done before, found a way to get themselves going on the back of their starting rotation. The Phillies didn't make it easy on themselves in September, going 10-14 down the stretch and needing to win their regular-season finale against the Rays to punch their ticket to the postseason. But now that they're in, this veteran group will look to show that they're better than the past month suggests.
Braves: It was a reassuring year in Atlanta, a much-needed reminder that no, this era of Braves baseball was not over after their disastrous, postseason-less 2025. A change in manager, from the now-retired Brian Snitker to the endearingly pugnacious Walt Weiss, set the tone. As did a major refresh of Atlanta's coaching staff. That turnover, in contrast with the continuity on the roster, proved crucial as Atlanta waltzed to its first division title since 2023.
Big campaigns from metronomic first baseman Matt Olson and 2025 NL Rookie of the Year Drake Baldwin shocked nobody. The same was true for ace Chris Sale, certain to be voted an NL Cy Young finalist. But few would've predicted Michael Harris II leading the team in bWAR with a dynamic, consistent offensive season. Role players such as Mauricio Dubón, Mike Yastrzemski and Dominic Smith all delivered critical production to help offset underwhelming seasons from the likes of Ozzie Albies and Austin Riley.
Ronald Acuña Jr., that wonderfully mercurial burst of baseballing light, might've fit into that last group if not for an otherworldly September in which he clocked seven homers with a .950 OPS. That renaissance continuing into October would be a game-changer for the Braves, whose 2021 title came with Acuña sidelined.
X-factors
Phillies: Trea Turner
The regular season wasn't kind to shortstop Trea Turner, who recorded the worst season of his career. But the thing about the postseason is that it allows players who have not yet written the final story on their season to become heroes. And if the Phillies want to move past Atlanta and reach the NLDS for the fifth straight year, Turner finding his rhythm would be a welcomed sight for the team's offense. Turner has a .733 OPS off Sale in 25 career at-bats and a very respectable .863 OPS off Mahle in 25 career at-bats.
Braves: Tyler Mahle
Chris Sale is going to start Game 1 for Atlanta, and he's probably going to be pretty good. That feels as bankable as anything in our topsy-turvy world. But Mahle, set to throw Game 2, has been one of the game's most reliable starters since he joined the Braves from a zip-less San Francisco team at the deadline. The veteran righty posted a 1.99 ERA with Atlanta, allowing one earned or fewer in seven of his nine starts.
Mahle's most recent start, however, was a relative stinker. He surrendered five runs and struck out just four at home against an undermanned Reds lineup. And the underlying metrics, it should be said, are a bit more skeptical about Mahle's prospects. That's understandable. He doesn't throw that hard or strike out oodles of hitters. He hasn't conjured more swing-and-miss or meaningfully lowered opponents' hard-hit rate as a Brave. And yet, Mahle has found a way to find outs. Whether he can do so against Philly's bats will be huge.
How they win
Phillies: Can any team in baseball go toe-to-toe with Philly's starting rotation? With the quartet of Wheeler, Sánchez, Luzardo and Nola, the Phillies should have the advantage in a three-, five- or seven-game series. So while their offense is more of a wild card (pun intended), this team should be able to count on its starter giving them a chance to win every time out. And if that foursome gets hot, it's not outlandish to believe they could carry Philly on another deep postseason run.
Braves: It has been a restful week for the Braves, who were able to sit back, relax and line up their starting rotation for this wild-card series. The same cannot be said for Philly, which needed every last out to clinch on the regular season's final day. For the Phillies, the sense of exhaustion is real and gives Atlanta a legitimate advantage.
But it all starts with Sale. If he cruises like he's capable of in Game 1, that puts Atlanta in the catbird seat. Only one team in the current playoff format (the 2025 Yankees) came back to win a wild-card series after losing the first game.
Series prediction: Braves in 3
No. 6 Chicago White Sox vs. No. 3 Houston Astros
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 5 p.m. ET Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): David Sandlin (CWS) vs. Peter Lambert (HOU)
Game 2 5 p.m. ET Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Sean Burke (CWS) vs. Hunter Brown (HOU)
Game 3, TBD*: Davis Martin (CWS) vs. Hayden Wesneski (HOU)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
White Sox: The White Sox have been easily one of the best stories of the 2026 regular season, reaching the postseason for the first time since 2021. Chicago became the first team in MLB history to reach the postseason following three consecutive 100-loss seasons, capturing the third AL wild-card spot. The offense, led by first-time All-Stars Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami, was the driving force behind the Sox's success. Chicago finished the season with a top-five offense in MLB.
The fact that the White Sox didn't win the AL Central might come as a disappointment, considering they were in first place for the majority of the second half. Still, it's undeniable that any result that puts them in the playoffs is a huge victory for the organization and a fan base that has been waiting for competitive baseball.
Astros: For a franchise that has accomplished so much over the past decade, there's something shameful, even humiliating about raising the 2026 AL West banner. That's because these Astros are, by record, the single worst division winner in the sport's long past. Before Sunday, no team with a .500 record or below had ever reached the postseason. But Houston rewrote history thanks to an MVP-caliber season from Yordan Alvarez and a tidal wave of mediocrity from its AL West counterparts. Their inclusion in the October jamboree is more an indictment of the Texas Rangers and the Seattle Mariners than anything else, but the Astros at least ended on a high note with their 9-0 win over the A's on Sunday.
Houston also deserves a morsel of credit for refurbishing its season after a disastrous April. Reaching .500 with the fourth-worst starting staff by ERA — only the Reds, A's and Rockies were worse — is also an accomplishment worth commending, a testament to something. Where would this club be without Peter Lambert, whose 3.87 ERA in 153 2/3 innings offered the only semblance of stability for a roster constantly in flux?
Things got sad enough, discombobulated enough, that in August owner Jim Crane relieved GM Dana Brown of his duties. There's an overwhelming expectation that skipper Joe Espada won't be back next year, either. It's difficult to be optimistic about Houston's very uncertain future. But in the random present of playoff baseball, anything is possible — especially when you employ the best hitter on the planet.
X-factors
White Sox: Munetaka Murakami
Munetaka Murakami is a game-changer, and his presence in the White Sox's lineup is a huge advantage in the postseason. The White Sox's rookie slugger burst onto the scene in 2026, hitting 35 home runs and providing instant impact in his first season after coming over from Japan. But following a midseason hamstring injury, the league seemed to adjust to him; Murakami finished with a slashline of .184/.328/.423 and 11 homers since Aug 1. Still, he has the type of power that can change a series by himself, and with three homers in the final week of the season, he appears to be coming out of his second-half slump. If Murakami has rediscovered his power stroke, it could change this series.
Astros: Isaac Paredes
Yordan Alvarez is currently the best hitter on earth. He cannot, under any circumstances, be allowed to dictate proceedings during this series. Chicago must make somebody else in Houston's mediocre lineup beat them. If there's a base open with Alvarez up, he should just stroll straight to first every time.
That puts a mountain of pressure on Paredes. The stocky third baseman has been hitting right behind Alvarez for most of the season and has, for the most part, showed well. He's a supremely weird hitter, one who rarely hits the ball hard or barrels it up. But Paredes doesn't whiff, doesn't punch out and has a preternatural knack for pulling the ball in the air. Expect him to come up multiple times in big spots with runners on.
How they win
White Sox: The White Sox's offense has carried them all season, and if they hope to advance to the ALDS against their division rival, they'll have to slug their way there. Vargas, Murakami and shortstop Colson Montgomery each finished the season with more than 30 longballs, and the Sox finished fifth in MLB in homers. For a team built to slug, Daikin Park in Houston isn't the worst environment to play in on the road. Chicago's power-packed lineup has shown that if they're hitting the ball out of the ballpark, offensively, they can play with anyone.
Astros: Houston desperately needs offensive contributions from someone besides Alvarez. Maybe it's the aforementioned Paredes or the en fuego Yainer Díaz. Perhaps Jose Altuve, 36 years old and in full decline, has one magical month left in his Hall of Fame career. But with such a tattered pitching staff, the Astros need to score to win. They also need to win the Hunter Brown start; he's far and away their best starter. They need a lot, frankly. And yet, much weirder October things have happened inside that East Texas thunderdome over the past decade.
Series prediction: Astros in 3
No. 5 Boston Red Sox vs. No. 4 New York Yankees
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 8 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Payton Tolle (BOS) vs. Cam Schlittler (NYY)
Game 2, 8 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Sonny Gray (BOS) vs. Max Fried (NYY)
Game 3, TBD*: Ranger Suárez (BOS) vs. Gerrit Cole (NYY)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Red Sox: Odysseus would be proud. What a winding, bizarre and tumultuous road it has been for the Sox. Boston began the year like a snail on Unisom, posting a lackluster 9-17 record through April 24. That precipitated a dramatic, Red Wedding-style culling, in which manager Alex Cora and several other staff members were relieved of their duties. Extended injury list stints for the team's two most important pieces, outfielder Roman Anthony and 2025 Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet, made a turnaround feel awfully unlikely. On July 24, the Sox lost a rubber match in Colorado and traveled home 14 games under .500. Their postseason odds wallowed around 10%.
Then, everything changed. It began with a home mop against the Yanks and fully kicked into gear when the Red Sox hit the road for a three-city swing the first week of July. They went 9-0 on that trip before winning six straight at home. That 15-game streak catapulted them back into contention and the good graces of an understandably unplugged fan base. Between July 3 and Aug. 7, the Sox went a ridiculous 32-5, trampolining from 14 games under .500 to 13 games over. Fenway was a zoo. Nothing could go wrong. Boston ballfans beamed once again.
The heater earned Cora's replacement, Chad Tracy, the full-time gig. It also afforded the Sox a relatively comfortable September. It's worth noting, though, that Boston has not played particularly crisply since cooling off from the volcanic run, with a 21-22 record since Aug. 8. Ultimately, their final numbers and standing in the American League are not shocking or unexpected, even though Boston's odyssey was wonky beyond comparison.
Yankees: For all the stress, the drama, the hand-wringing, for all the injuries and under-performance, 2026 was a relatively straightforward season in YankeeLand. A lot, it should be said, went wrong. Reigning AL MVP Aaron Judge has played just seven games since May. Giancarlo Stanton hasn't played since April. Max Fried and Carlos Rodón each missed about two months. Young players such as Anthony Volpe, Jasson Dominguez and Austin Wells regressed offensively. Gerrit Cole, coming back from Tommy John, didn't fully recapture his frontline best.
And yet, here the Yankees are, with 93 wins and in an identical place to where they finished last year. That's thanks to breakout campaigns from homegrown pieces such as Cam Schlittler (the AL Cy Young favorite) and Ben Rice (41 home runs and a .897 OPS). Closer David Bednar has been dynamite. Cody Bellinger has been a rock. Skipper Aaron Boone kept the train on the tracks. Three games at home against the Red Sox await. Beyond that looms an ALDS against a daunting division foe. We've been here before.
The largest difference, of course, is the uncertainty swirling around Judge. The Yankees' captain missed three months due to a rib problem, came back for a week, strained his calf and went back on the shelf. Boone says he's preparing for a wild-card round without Judge. Judge says he plans to play. What sort of magic this reduced version of Judge can conjure is easily the juiciest storyline ahead of this rivalry showdown. That said, this series, like this Yankees season, is probably going to be dictated by the pitchers.
X-factors
Red Sox: Roman Anthony
It has been an odd season for the 22-year-old, who missed last year's wild-card festivities due to injury. In March, Anthony was a late addition to Team USA's WBC roster. He shined on that grand stage, impressing his more established teammates and earning plaudits from a coaching staff of hardball lifers. That only ratcheted up the hype on a player expected to carry a franchise less than a year after he became legally permitted to drink a beer.
So when Anthony started slowly, disappointment bubbled. Then, on May 4, he tore a ligament in his finger; that kept him out of action until Aug. 30. A lot happened in the interim, most of which Anthony spent rehabbing at the team's complex in Florida. Since returning, he has looked promising, tantalizingly close to unleashing the full assortment of his talents upon the league. Now, with Willson Contreras banged up and either unavailable or restricted, the pressure returns to Anthony's young shoulders.
Yankees: Luis García Jr.
García was a curious character for the Yankees to shape their trade deadline around. Instead of acquiring a piece that filled an obvious void (righty stick with defensive value or versatility), GM Brian Cashman opted to add the most dynamic hitter possible. New York landed on García, who was in the midst of an offensive breakout under a new Washington Nationals regime.
For a month, that plan bore fruit, with the Dominican slugger posting an .846 OPS in August. But since then, the wheels have fallen off, with García's chase rate skyrocketing. His September OPS started with a 5. He has homered just twice since Aug. 26. He doesn't have an extra-base hit since Sept. 10. There's a chance, given Boston's bevy of southpaws and New York's DH surplus, that he doesn't start every game. But García will get his chances, and whether he comes up big might swing the series.
How they win
Red Sox: Boston's pitching staff is the only one in baseball that ranks in the top five in both home run rate and walk rate. That's a rare combo. Usually, throwing the ball in the strike zone more often leads to more hard contact. But these Red Sox hurlers, for whatever reason, have threaded that needle perfectly. No team in the league has allowed fewer homers. However, no team has hit more than the Yankees. Boston revitalized its season behind pitching and defense, keeping the scores low and the games close. Doing so here will give them the best chance of authoring an upset.
Yankees: No American League team can compete with New York's starting staff. But the Yankees need more than dominance from Schlittler, Fried and Cole. They need length. The bridge to Bednar is unsteady. So the longer the starters go, the rosier that path looks. Offensively, the Yankees need a big swing or two from their right-handed bats against Boston's left-handed arms. That could come from a banged-up Judge or Stanton. It could come from veteran southpaw-killer Paul Goldschmidt, trade-acquisition Heliot Ramos or rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. If it comes from the beleaguered Anthony Volpe, the tri-state area will lose its collective marbles. But somebody, anybody who stands on the right side of the batter's box has to make an impact.
Series prediction: Yankees in 3
No. 5 Chicago Cubs vs. No. 4 San Diego Padres
(all times ET)
Projected starters
Game 1, 10 p.m. Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): Shota Imanaga (CHC) vs. Michael King (SD)
Game 2, 10 p.m. Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Clay Holmes (CHC) vs. Nick Pivetta (SD)
Game 3, TBD*: Matthew Boyd (CHC) vs. Walker Buehler or Casey Mize or Robbie Ray (SD)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Cubs: It was Pete Crow-Armstrong's world, and the rest of us just lived in it. Chicago's 24-year-old center fielder went fully supersonic this year, cranking 45 homers, swiping 41 bags and delivering a .945 OPS with his typically elite outfield defense. He will win the NL MVP, and it might be unanimous. That performance shaped and guided and defined this Cubs' season, electrifying an offense that led baseball in OPS, K/BB rate and runs per game.
Alex Bregman's arrival via free agency, too, cannot be understated. He struggled mightily for the first few months, with his extended schneid at one point eliciting boos from a frustrated Wrigley crowd. But since July 12, Bregman leads all qualified National League hitters in OPS. His experience, comportment and leadership, by all accounts, have also had a meaningful impact on Crow-Armstrong.
But pitching woes, in both the rotation and the bullpen, kept Chicago from ever seriously threatening the Brewers for the NL Central title. The Cubs started the year on something of a roller coaster, with two 10-game winning streaks and a 10-game losing streak before the calendar flipped to June. They'll enter October on something of an ice floe, with 15 runs scored in their final six contests.
Padres: San Diego has the best record in baseball since July 24. The day before, the Pads lost a rubber match in Atlanta to fall to three games under. 500. That pushed the club four games adrift of a wild-card spot, with the Cardinals, Pirates, Marlins, Nationals and Diamondbacks standing between them and a trip to October. That was the low-water mark for this team.
Since that date, the Padres have gone 41-18. They won five straight in late July, six straight in August and eight straight in September. They've lost thrice since Labor Day. The reason for the resurgence? Check out these numbers.
| Padres offensive ranks before and after July 24 | | |
| | Before | After |
| Runs/game | 4.14 (25th) | 4.95 (3rd) |
| AVG | .230 (28th) | .268 (2nd) |
| OBP | .307 (27th) | .339 (2nd) |
| SLG | .383 (27th) | .425 (2nd) |
| OPS | .689 (26th) | .764 (2nd) |
San Diego's offense went from bottom-five to top-five. Some of that is batted-ball luck and sequencing. A lot of it is Fernando Tatis Jr. turning back into a monster. Jackson Merrill had a similar rebirth. Ty France continued his bounce-back campaign. Xander Bogaerts shifted from unwatchable to capable. Unsung heroes such as Dustin Harris and Luis Rengifo got hot. The starting pitching did just enough. The game's best bullpen never stopped dominating. It's that unit, led by a cadre of flamethrowers in Mason Miller, Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez, that makes these Padres a particularly formidable October opponent.
X-factors
Cubs: Alex Bregman — specifically, his face
One week ago, Bregman was the victim of some very painful misfortune. A check-swing foul ball off the bat of Cubs first baseman Michael Busch struck Bregman in the face while he was standing in the on-deck circle. Blood dripped from below his left eye as he scurried down the dugout steps into the clubhouse. A trip to the hospital revealed multiple facial fractures. The incident kept Bregman out of the lineup until Friday, when he went 0-for-4 with a strikeout as Chicago's DH. He went 4-for-4 with two home runs and a walk in Sunday's season finale.
There's no doubt that Bregman, the textbook definition of a "grinder," will take the field in October. But at what level? He has been so integral to Chicago's lineup for the past few months that even a slightly reduced version of Bregman could unsettle things. Among active players, only his former Astros teammate Jose Altuve has taken more postseason plate appearances.
Padres: Fernando Tatis Jr.
Nothing is more meaningfully different about this year's Padres team compared to the one that went three and see-ya at Wrigley in 2025 than Fernando Tatis Jr.'s stunning offensive reemergence. Things didn't start so swimmingly this year for the swaggering outfielder, who needed 55 games to clock his first longball of this season. But since May 30, Tatis' .914 OPS ranks fourth in the NL, and his 4.9 fWAR ranks second in MLB behind only Crow-Armstrong.
This version of Tatis looks a lot like the one who took the baseball world by storm en route to finishing third in NL MVP in 2021. Will that brilliance show up in a small October sample? It usually has throughout the 27-year-old's career; he holds a 1.114 postseason OPS in 70 plate appearances. Tatis, though, has never advanced past the NLDS. Remember, he was in PED timeout when the Padres stampeded to the NLCS in 2022. Could this month be his path back to full-blown superstardom?
How they win
Cubs: The margins were razor thin when these teams lined up in the wild-card round last year, with a highlight reel of web gems from shortstop Dansby Swanson making the difference. Those games, oddly enough, were incredibly low-scoring, with Chicago snagging two 3-1 wins and San Diego edging out a 3-0 win. It's hard to imagine the Cubs and their underwhelming relief group winning that way again, particularly on the road. To advance, they'll need buckets of runs. With PCA, Bregman, Seiya Suzuki and Co., that's a real possibility.
Padres: The Padres' formula for success has been the same for the past few seasons: Shorten the game. San Diego realistically needs five innings from its starters. Then manager Craig Stammen gets to turn things over to the best relief core in baseball, led by southpaw Adrían Morejon and flamethrower Mason Miller. The Friars' starting pitching has gotten stronger as they've gotten healthy, so if Michael King in Game 1 and likely Nick Pivetta in Game 2 can each give San Diego 15 outs, the Padres have a good chance of making quick work of Chicago.

Sep 25, 2026, 9:16 PM ET
Seattle Mariners relief pitcher Andres Munoz (knee) was placed on the 15-day Injured List on Friday, Ryan Divish reports. Munoz hasn't pitched since Sunday, and now goes to the shelf due to right knee inflammation. His inconsistent 2026 season will now come to an end with a few games left in the regular season. He'll finish the season with a 4.24 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, and an 89/24 K/BB ratio with 28 saves across 57.2 innings of work. The expectation is that Jose A. Ferrer and Seranthony Dominguez will work in save situations over the final few days of the regular season. Fantasy managers should expect Munoz to be back in the closer role and fully healthy for the start of next season.--Andy Webb
Source: Ryan Divish
More Recent News
Xavier Edwards Still Out for Marlins


Keith Hernandez




Sep 25, 2026, 6:07 PM ET
Miami Marlins middle infielder Xavier Edwards (thumb) remains out of the starting nine for Friday's series opener at home against the division-rival Atlanta Braves, per MLB.com. Jared Serna will make another start at second base for the Fish and will hit in the nine-hole against Braves left-hander Ray Kerr. This will be Edwards' fifth straight missed game after he aggravated a left-thumb injury last Saturday against the San Diego Padres. The Marlins have not rushed the 27-year-old back after being eliminated from playoff contention. At this point, he only has two more chances to return before the end of the regular season on Saturday and Sunday against Atlanta. The switch-hitting middle infielder was having a second straight solid season for the Fish this year, slashing .280/.360/.371 with a .730 OPS, a career-high six home runs, 52 RBI, 21 stolen bases, and 61 runs scored across 142 games and 595 plate appearances. You are not going to get any power from Edwards, but he remains useful for his speed and contact-oriented approach at the dish in fantasy leagues.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Luis Arraez Out on Friday, Report "Not a Great One"


Keith Hernandez




Sep 25, 2026, 6:01 PM ET
Philadelphia Phillies infielder Luis Arraez (ankle) is out of the team's starting lineup on Friday against the visiting Tampa Bay Rays, and the report on his ankle injury from Thursday night is "not a great one," interim manager Don Mattingly told Scott Lauber of The Philadelphia Inquirer. Mattingly did not give a grade on the sprain, and the Phillies have not decided on an injured-list placement, which would take Arraez out until at least Oct. 5, or around Game 3 of the divisional round. X-rays on Arraez's left ankle came back negative on Thursday night, but his sprained ankle is still stiff and sore, which is why he will not play on Friday. Bryson Stott is at second base and batting fifth on Friday, with Edmundo Sosa at third base and hitting ninth against Rays right-hander Freddy Peralta. The Phillies would obviously love to avoid putting the 29-year-old All-Star on the IL, but if he cannot play at all this weekend, they might have no choice. The four-time All-Star and three-time batting champion has hit only .278 (49-for-176) in his 46 games with the Phillies this year after being traded from the San Francisco Giants in early August, but he is still the league's leading hitter at .310 overall. Not having Arraez available next week for the start of the playoffs (if the Phillies qualify) would be a big loss for Philadelphia.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Philadelphia Inquirer - Scott Lauber
Zyhir Hope Appears To Be Future Fantasy Star


Brian Buckey




Sep 25, 2026, 1:46 PM ET
Detroit Tigers new top outfield prospect Zyhir Hope showed off plenty of promise with Double-A Erie following his trade from the Dodgers in the Tarik Skubal deal. Hope was the headline piece coming back to Detroit after dealing away their ace, and he proved his potential with a massive minor-league season at the Double-A level between the Dodgers and Tigers. The 21-year-old left-handed hitter combined to hit .287 with 29 homers and 111 RBI to go with 86 runs scored and 26 stolen bases. Hope has a 50-grade hit tool with 60-grade power and 55-grade speed. The future is bright for Hope, and he could make his debut with the Tigers in 2027. Expect the five-category skills Hope has shown in the minors to translate to the big leagues, making him a great target for fantasy managers as soon as next season.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller
Source: Minor League Baseball
Caden Hunter Looks Like Future Fantasy Ace


Brian Buckey




Sep 25, 2026, 1:38 PM ET
Baltimore Orioles pitching prospect Caden Hunter turned in a dominant 2026 minor-league season between three levels. Finishing up at Double-A Chesapeake in his age-22 season, Hunter combined to pitch to a 5-3 record with a 2.01 ERA and 1.06 WHIP with 151 strikeouts in 103 innings pitched. In his first professional season out of USC, Hunter dominated to hold opposing hitters to a .171 batting average. The 6-foot-2, 205-pound left-hander is the No. 4 overall prospect of the Orioles and boasts a 60-grade fastball and a 55-grade slider and changeup combination with a 45-grade curveball. Hunter looks like a future fantasy star with the size and skills to be a dominant force on the mound with the Orioles in the future. Look for more of Hunter in the minors in 2027, with the potential to make his MLB debut as soon as next season.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller
Source: Minor League Baseball
Sep 25, 2026, 1:27 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers pitching prospect Christian Zazueta combined between High-A Great Lakes and Double-A Tulsa to have a stellar age-21 minor-league season in 2026. Zazueta's overall numbers ended up very good, with a combined 6-4 record, 3.65 ERA, and 0.97 WHIP with 144 strikeouts in 103 2/3 innings. The 6-foot-3 right-hander limited opposing batters to a .214 batting average. He is the No. 5 prospect in the Dodgers' system with a 60-grade fastball and changeup combination with a 50-grade secondary pitch in his slider. Zazueta shows very good control and looks to have all the tools to be a future fantasy-relevant pitcher. It could be a few years before Zazueta makes his MLB debut, but he looks like a great dynasty-league addition in the near term.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller

Connelly Early to Pitch This Weekend


Keith Hernandez




Sep 25, 2026, 1:26 PM ET
Washington Nationals left-hander Connelly Early (elbow) threw 40 pitches across 1 2/3 innings with Triple-A Rochester on Sept. 20 and will come off the 60-day injured list to make one more start this season this weekend against the division-rival New York Mets, according to MLB.com. Early landed on the injured list on July 1 and was moved to the 60-day IL on Aug. 22 due to inflammation in his left elbow. It will be his first start with the Nationals after the team acquired him from the Boston Red Sox at the trade deadline in early August. In his 17 starts (91 2/3 innings pitched) for the BoSox this year in his second season in the big leagues, Early went 7-5 with a 3.44 ERA (4.60 FIP) and 1.25 WHIP with 93 strikeouts and 34 walks. He had a 2.33 ERA and 1.09 WHIP in a smaller sample size of only four starts in his first taste of the big leagues near the end of the 2025 campaign. Early, a fifth-rounder from Virginia in 2023, is one of the more intriguing young lefty arms in baseball, but he will be far too risky in starting fantasy lineups with championships on the line this weekend against New York after his long injury layoff. UPDATE: Early will make his Nationals debut on Saturday.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Sep 25, 2026, 1:19 PM ET
Detroit Tigers catcher prospect Josue Briceno overcame wrist surgery and battled a late ankle injury in what was an injury-plagued age 22 minor league season. Briceno combined between four minor-league levels in 2026 to combine for a .250 batting average with nine homers and 29 RBI and 23 runs in 42 total games. Briceno played 15 games at Triple-A Toledo and hit just .196 in a very small sample size. He hit .297 in 17 games at Double-A Erie prior to his call up to Toledo. Briceno is the No. 4 prospect of the Tigers and has a 50-grade hit tool with 60-grade power. The catcher position is in good shape in Detroit with All-Star Dillon Dingler and Eduardo Valencia. Briceno is a power bat with limited speed that could potentially shift to first base or find a spot at DH if needed, but he is still a big part of the future plans for Tigers brass and could make a 2027 debut.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller
Source: Minor League Baseball
Sep 25, 2026, 1:10 PM ET
Washington Nationals shortstop prospect Devin Fitz-Gerald split his minor-league season between two levels but finished with nice overall numbers in his age-21 season. Between High-A Wilmington and Double-A Harrisburg, Fitz-Gerald combined to hit .251 with 20 homers and 67 RBI, along with 15 stolen bases and 78 runs scored. The switch-hitter was originally drafted by the Texas Rangers and came to the Nationals organization in the MacKenzie Gore trade. Fitz-Gerald is the No. 5 prospect for the Nationals and has a 50-grade hit tool with 50-grade power and 45-grade speed. Fitz-Gerald looks like he could be an impact player for the Nationals, but Washington does have another elite shortstop prospect in Seaver King, so Fitz-Gerald's future could involve another infield position.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller
Source: Minor League Baseball
Sep 25, 2026, 1:01 PM ET
Tampa Bay Rays first base prospect Xavier Isaac had a good minor league season at age 22 and closed it off well with a good stint at Triple-A Durham. Called up to Durham from Double-A Montgomery on August 25, Isaac played 18 games with the Durham Bulls down the stretch. He finished that stint with three homers and eight RBI in 59 at bats with a .271 batting average and 11 runs scored. Altogether between Montgomery and Durham, Isaac combined to hit .258 with 27 homers and 79 RBI to go with 20 stolen bases and 88 runs scored. Isaac is the No. 18 prospect in the Rays system and looks like he could be ready for a role on the 2027 Rays team. Isaac appears to be a promising talent with 60-grade power, but just a 35-grade hit tool. He could be a good homer and RBI threat but leave something to be desired in the batting average category.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller
Source: Minor League Baseball
Sep 25, 2026, 11:38 AM ET

item.content:encoded:
MIAMI -- Now that Austin Riley has created some encouragement by homering a couple times this week, should the Braves’ third baseman begin every week of the postseason by undergoing an emergency root canal?
“No, I wouldn’t wish that on my worst enemy,” Riley said.
Riley’s bid to homer in a third straight game proved unsuccessful in a 3-0 loss to the Marlins on Friday night at loanDepot park. But having homered against the Reds on Wednesday and Thursday, it’s safe to say this week has progressed much better than it started.
An intense toothache woke Riley around 5 a.m. CT on Sunday in his Houston hotel. The Braves arranged for him to visit a dentist, who was unable to do the root canal because of staffing issues. After returning to Daikin Park, the two-time All-Star felt incredible pain after biting into a sandwich.
Braves head athletic trainer George Poulis then arranged for Riley to visit another dentist, who completed the root canal and sent the slugger back to the stadium in time to be with his teammates as they celebrated clinching the NL East.
“My face was half numb, but it was all good,” Riley said.
Unfortunately for Riley, he hasn’t been numb to the frustration he has felt while producing career lows in both batting average (.222) and OPS (.662). He’s also set a franchise single-season record with a career-high 197 strikeouts, two of which were registered as Eury Pérez dazzled the Braves with a one-hit shutout on Friday.
With four homers in his past 18 games, Riley needs to go deep just one time in the regular season’s final two games to secure a 20-homer season. That’s a satisfying number when you consider he hit just nine in the season’s first 95 games. But this is a guy who tallied three straight 30-homer seasons from 2021-23.
“I don’t even look at [the stats] anymore,” Riley said. “At this point, it’s about, ‘What can I do today, and what can I do going forward?’”
When the Braves begin the Wild Card Series on Tuesday at Truist Park, Riley will be working with a new slate. If he gets hot and helps Atlanta advance deep into the postseason, he can distance himself from what he has done over the past six months.
“Austin's great,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “You never know if he's had an MVP season or if he's struggling. He’s the same guy. I know, obviously, he's been working really hard all year to try to turn things around, and I think he's trending the right way.”
Riley has been far more productive during the season’s second half. But the strikeout rate has been more alarming.
Pre-All-Star break: .207 BA, 9 HRs (38.1 At-bats per homer), .618 OPS, 29.4% strikeout rate
Post-AS break: .247 BA, 10 HRs (21.5 AB/HR), .734 OPS, 35.6% K rate
September: .222 BA, 4 HRs (18 AB/HR) .695 OPS, 32.9% K rate
Burdened by an abundance of video analysis and analytical data, Riley has been looking to simplify both his swing and his mindset. He knows he has looked robotic with many of his swings this year. But he feels good about an adjustment he made last weekend, when he noticed his right shoulder seemed to be tense and pointed inward with his stance.
Riley has spent the past few games focused on keeping that shoulder loose, with the hope he reduces the frequency with which he has pushed the bat through the zone or flipped the bat through the zone. His aim has been to make his swing look more natural.
“I definitely think this is the most confident I’ve been in a while with some of [the] cues and with some of the swings I’ve taken,” Riley said.

ATLANTA (AP) — Chris Sale struck out 10 and reached 200 Ks for the season, Mauricio Dubón delivered a winning RBI single in the 10th inning, and the Atlanta Braves defeated the Cincinnati Reds 3-2 on Wednesday night.
Matt Olson and Austin Riley hit solo homers for the Braves. Brent Suter (3-2) worked a scoreless 10th inning and earned the win.
Sale went 5 2/3 innings and was removed after recording his third strikeout of the game of Reds rookie Sal Stewart. The 37-year-old left-hander has reached 200 strikeouts nine times, which is the most of any pitcher since 2013. In his final start before the postseason, he allowed one run on four hits. Sale hit at least 99 mph on the radar gun on 12 of his 97 pitches.
Olson’s home run was his 41st of the season and tied the game at 1 in the sixth. Riley's homer tied the game at 2 in the seventh. Dubón was 2 for 4 with a walk and extended his hitting streak to 10 games.
Reds right fielder Juan Brito led off the game with a home run to center field off Sale. He went 2 for 4, including his third homer of the season.
Braves reliever Robert Suarez pitched for the first time since June 19 after being sidelined due to elbow inflammation. He pitched the seventh inning and gave up a leadoff triple to Matt McLain and a sacrifice fly to Will Banfield that gave the Reds a 2-1 lead. He threw 13 pitches.
Braves right fielder Ronald Acuña Jr. sat out after suffering a bone bruise when he fouled a ball off his shin in Tuesday's 4-0 loss to the Reds. Braves manager Walt Weiss said Acuña was asking to play and felt he could play right field Wednesday, but the Braves decided to be cautious with a postseason berth clinched.
Up next
Braves RHP Tyler Mahle (7-10, 3.81) will make his final start before the postseason against Reds RHP Brady Singer (6-15, 5.67) in the series finale Thursday.

In what will likely be his last regular season start for the Atlanta Braves this season, Chris Sale will be facing off against Andrew Abbott and the Cincinnati Reds.
Chris Sale is not the front runner for the Cy Young award, but will most certainly get some second and third place votes with his 2.18 ERA, 30.3 percent strikeout rate, and league leading strikeout to walk ratio of 6.13. Sale also leads the NL is best HR rate of 0.5 per nine innings, and best walk rate in the NL of 4.9 percent.
Side note, Chris Sale has the best career strikeout to walk ratio of all-time. Sale has also pitched 157.0 innings thus far this season, which is hurting his Cy Young chances to guys like Jacob Misiorowski. It could be argued that he has passed his fellow competitor Cristopher Sánchez, but Sánchez has a whopping 200.0 IP which is second in MLB behind Sandy Alcantara.
The Braves got a scare yesterday when Ronald Acuña fouled a ball off his shin, but luckily all the tests came back negative. The Braves have already clinched the division so a loss to the Reds yesterday was not a huge deal except the chances of a playoff bye are quickly fading. The offense looked bad again, so hopefully they can catch a spark again before the playoffs take off.
No Braves player has faced Abbott more than five at-bats. Ha-Seong Kim has a HR in his four at-bats and Ozzie Albies has a .600 average. Michael Harris has struggled to an OPS of .400 in his five at-bats, and Mauricio Dubón and Mike Yastrzemski are hitless in their three at-bats. Austin Riley is also hitless in five at-bats.
It is hard to make any type of prediction on such a limited history, but we can look at Abbott's numbers and see his 4.70 ERA is approximately eleven percent below average and his 1.472 WHIP is the worst of his four year career. This season he has struggled with walks giving up 4.2 per nine innings. The Braves need to be patient this even and take advantage of his weakness. It is no secret that the Braves struggle in the walk department. Their 7.7 percent is the third worst in MLB. To be fair, they strike out at a lower rate than the average team this season, but walks get runners on base to knock in.
The Reds are in the bottom six in RP ERA this season. The Braves have feasted on RPs all season long. The key to the game tonight seems to be be patient against Abbott because he gives up a lot of walks. Get to the bullpen, and strike. Chris Sale should keep the runs low to make this a pretty easy win on paper.
